$comment: Scotland, Human Rights Law - the distinctive double bind under both the Human Rights Act 1998 (UK-wide) and the Scotland Act 1998 s.57(2), a free-standing devolution-competence limit distinct from the HRA itself: a member of the Scottish Government has no power to act incompatibly with Convention rights. Cadder v HM Advocate is the leading illustration - it forced emergency Scottish legislation within days of judgment.

authorities.name: Scotland Act 1998, section 57(2)
authorities.date_note: Royal Assent date. The Scotland Act 2012 substituted 'Scottish Government' for 'Scottish Executive', in force from 3 July 2012. The original subsection also barred incompatibility 'with Community law' - the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 omitted that limb, in force from 31 December 2020, leaving Convention-rights incompatibility as the sole surviving limit.
authorities.proposition: A member of the Scottish Government has no power to make any subordinate legislation, or to do any other act, so far as the legislation or act is incompatible with any of the Convention rights - a free-standing devolution-competence limit on the executive, distinct from and additional to the Human Rights Act 1998's own s.6 unlawful-act provision. Section 57(3) carves out an exception for the Lord Advocate's acts in prosecuting offences or as head of the systems of criminal prosecution and investigation of deaths - meaning the Lord Advocate's prosecutorial decisions are NOT exempted from the s.57(2) Convention-rights limit for other purposes, which is precisely why Cadder was framed as an s.57(2)/(3) devolution-competence challenge rather than only an ordinary HRA claim.

authorities.name: Cadder v HM Advocate
authorities.citation: Cadder v HM Advocate [2010] UKSC 43; 2011 SC (UKSC) 13; 2010 SLT 1125
authorities.court: UK Supreme Court, on a Scottish appeal
authorities.judge_or_panel: Lord Hope (Deputy President, leading judgment), Lord Rodger, Lord Walker, Lord Brown, Lord Mance, Lord Kerr, Sir John Dyson SCJ - unanimous
authorities.proposition: The appellant challenged the Lord Advocate's leading and relying on evidence of his police interview, framed expressly as ultra vires under Scotland Act 1998 s.57(2) and (3) read with Human Rights Act 1998 s.6(2), on the ground that he had no access to legal advice before questioning, contrary to article 6(3)(c) read with article 6(1) ECHR (applying the Grand Chamber's ruling in Salduz v Turkey). Lord Hope, para 63: 'I would hold that the decisions of the High Court of Justiciary in Paton v Ritchie 2000 JC 271, Dickson v HM Advocate 2001 JC 203 and HM Advocate v McLean 2010 SLT 73 are no longer good law in the light of the Grand Chamber's ruling in Salduz and that they should be overruled. I would allow the appeal on the ground that leading and relying on the evidence of the appellant's interview by the police was a violation of his rights under article 6(3)(c) read in conjunction with article 6(1) of the Convention.' The case was remitted to the High Court of Justiciary for further procedure rather than the conviction being quashed outright (para 64). The ruling affected an estimated 76,000 pending or ongoing cases and forced the Scottish Government to pass emergency legislation (the Criminal Procedure (Legal Assistance, Detention and Appeals) (Scotland) Act 2010) within days.

what_this_is_not: Two nodes covering the s.57(2) Convention-rights limit on the Scottish Government/Lord Advocate and its application in Cadder. Does not cover s.29(2)(d)'s parallel legislative-competence limit on the Scottish Parliament itself (touched on only in passing), the Human Rights Act 1998's own separate framework as it applies UK-wide, or any other Scots human-rights subject - all remain unbuilt.
